title: Treatment for aplastic anaemia | NHS inform
text:
Treatment for aplastic anaemia
If you have aplastic anaemia, your treatment will usually be managed by haematologists. They are specialist blood doctors.
Treatments will be tailored to your individual needs and can vary depending on:
how severe your aplastic anaemia is
your age
your general health
if you have any underlying health conditions
Research on treatments for aplastic anaemia is ongoing.
General approach to treatment of patients with aplastic anaemia
The general approach to treatment for patients with aplastic anaemia involves:
Looking for any specific causes.
Stopping any medications or drugs that might have contributed to the problem.
Providing supportive care to treat symptoms and reduce the risk of bleeding and infections.
Considering definitive therapy with immunosuppression or stem cell transplant.
Supportive care
Supportive care aims to treat symptoms of aplastic anaemia. It involves different treatments depending on how severe the condition is. For example, you may need blood or platelet transfusions, and/or medicines to help prevent infections.
Treatment for non-severe aplastic anaemia
If you have aplastic anaemia that isn’t severe, your treatment will be tailored to your needs. This can involve supportive care.
Supportive care for non-severe aplastic anaemia means you may need:
to stop any medications that could be causing a low blood count
blood transfusions
medication – if you’re struggling with recurring infections
watch and wait (you may also hear this called careful monitoring)
Some patients may be offered immuno-suppressive treatment (IST) with therapies that are designed to suppress your immune system to allow your bone marrow to recover. This might include medicines like
anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG)
and ciclosporin.
Watch and wait
Watch and wait is for people with non-severe aplastic anaemia who don’t need active treatment. Your healthcare team will monitor you closely and will discuss any changes with you.
You may hear watch and wait called other things when you’re in hospital. For example, “careful monitoring”.
Treatment for severe and very severe aplastic anaemia
If you have severe or very severe aplastic anaemia, you will receive supportive care. This means that you may need:
to stop any medications that could be contributing to a low blood count
blood or platelet transfusion to maintain your blood count
medicines to prevent infection
These treatments are likely to be ongoing.
In addition, patients with severe or very severe aplastic anaemia will usually need definitive treatment to allow the bone marrow to recover.
Definitive treatment involves either a
stem cell transplant
or immuno-suppressive treatment (IST). Which treatment you receive will depend on your age, health and the availability of a stem cell donor.
Anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG)
Some people with aplastic anaemia may be treated with
anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG)
. This is usually given in hospital over a few days through an infusion or drip.
ATG works against T cells, which are an important part of the immune system. In people with aplastic anaemia, T cells target the bone marrow. ATG helps to reduce T cells which helps bone marrow recover from the damage.
ATG is usually combined with a tablet immunosuppressant called
Ciclosporin.
It’s likely that you’ll need to continue taking this for about a year.
Some patients may also be offered other treatments like
Eltrombopag
. This is a medication that stimulates stem cell and platelet production.
Effects of treatment
The treatments for aplastic anaemia can be significant and there can be a long recovery time.
There are many possible side effects from immunosuppressive therapy. Your doctor will discuss these with you before you begin treatment.
The biggest issue is that immunosuppression will make you more vulnerable to infection. This means you’ll need to be careful about infection risks.
Patients on immunosuppressive therapy will need to be monitored closely. They’ll also need regular blood tests to check for any problems.
Some people with aplastic anaemia may be considered for a stem cell transplant. This depends on:
the severity of your aplastic anaemia
your underlying health and fitness
the availability of a suitable donor
Having a stem cell transplant is a complex process. If you live in Scotland and this is being considered, you’ll be referred to the allogeneic stem cell transplant service in Glasgow. You’ll have detailed discussions about the process and counselling about how a stem cell transplant might impact on you.
Get further advice on stem cell transplant for aplastic anaemia
Talking about your treatment
When discussing your treatment, you may hear healthcare professionals talk about the following things.
Hickman line
Hickman (‘hick’) line is a type of central line or central venous catheter. It’s used for giving drugs or taking blood.
PICC line
A PICC line is a long, thin, flexible tube inserted into one of the large veins of the arm above the elbow. The line is then threaded into the vein until the tip of it sits in a large vein just above the heart.
Treatment for children and young people
The Aplastic Anaemia Trust has further information on
aplastic anaemia treatments for children and young people.
